title: How name etymology works - master names reference
description: Name etymology traces a name back through its root words: the earliest recorded form, the language family it belongs to, and the sound changes that shaped it on the way down. A claim like 'James means supplanter' is shorthand for a chain — Hebrew Ya'aqov, through Greek Iakobos and Latin Iacomus, into Old French and English. Good etymology cites each link; this database records the chain, not just the gloss.

title: Patronymic surnames worldwide - master names reference
description: Across cultures, 'son of' became a surname: English -son (Johnson), Scottish and Irish Mac and O' (MacDonald, O'Brien), Arabic ibn (Ibn Battuta), Russian -ovich/-evich, Spanish -ez (Fernandez, 'son of Fernando'), Polish -wicz, Scandinavian -sen/-sson. The pattern is the same everywhere — a father's given name frozen into a family name — while the marker word changes by language.

title: Occupational surnames worldwide - master names reference
description: Jobs became last names on every continent: Smith, Schmidt, Kowalski, and Ferrari all mean the smith; Taylor, Weber, and Haddad name the tailor, weaver, and blacksmith; Fischer and Shepherd name the fisher and herder. When a village needed to tell two Johns apart, the trade did the job, and the trade name stuck for centuries.

title: Descriptive surnames - master names reference
description: Before surnames were inherited, people were told apart by description: Brown and Rossi for coloring, Short and Long for build, Young for the younger of two same-named men. These bynames hardened into family names, which is why descriptive surnames now travel with families that no longer match the description.

title: Place-based surnames - master names reference
description: Many surnames are addresses in disguise: Hill and Dubois ('of the wood') for where a family lived, Van den Berg ('from the mountain') and Yamamoto ('base of the mountain') for the landmark nearby, London and York for the town left behind. Toponymic surnames map the migration of ordinary families.

title: Chinese naming conventions - master names reference
description: Chinese names put the family name first — Wang Wei is Mr. Wang — followed by a one- or two-character given name. Siblings often share a generation character, one syllable picked for their whole generation, and parents choose characters for meaning and stroke balance. The same characters are read differently across Mandarin, Cantonese, Wu, Min Nan, and Hakka.

title: Arabic naming conventions - master names reference
description: A classical Arabic name is a chain: the ism (personal name, e.g. Muhammad), the nasab (lineage — ibn/bint, 'son/daughter of'), the kunya (Abu/Umm, 'father/mother of' the eldest child), and the nisba (origin or trade, e.g. Al-Farsi, 'the Persian'). Modern use often shortens the chain to given name plus family name.

title: Spanish and Portuguese naming - master names reference
description: Spanish speakers traditionally carry two surnames — the father's first surname followed by the mother's first surname — so both family lines stay visible for a generation. Portuguese order flips them: mother's family name first, father's last. The -ez ending (Lopez, Fernandez) is the old Spanish patronymic, 'son of'.

title: Russian naming - master names reference
description: A full Russian name has three parts: given name, patronymic, and surname — Ivan Ivanovich Petrov is Ivan, son of Ivan, of the Petrov family. Surnames take gendered endings (-ov/-ova, -sky/-skaya), and friends use diminutives (Sasha for Aleksandr) that are names in their own right socially.

title: Korean naming - master names reference
description: Korean names are usually three syllables: a one-syllable family name (Kim, Lee, Park) followed by a two-syllable given name. The given name's meaning is fixed by the hanja (Chinese characters) chosen for it — the same sound Min-jun can mean different things with different hanja — and siblings often share one generation syllable, the dollimja.

title: Icelandic naming - master names reference
description: Iceland still uses a living patronymic system instead of inherited surnames: Jon's son is Jonsson, his daughter is Jonsdottir. Phone books sort by first name, and a naming committee approves new given names for grammar and tradition. It is the closest modern system to how most of Europe named people a thousand years ago.

title: South Asian naming conventions - master names reference
description: South Asian naming runs on several tracks at once: Sikh men take Singh ('lion') and women Kaur ('princess'); Tamil names often use a patronymic initial plus given name; Marathi surnames like Kulkarni and Deshmukh record old village offices; Sindhi surnames add -ani ('of', as in Advani). The surname usually encodes community, office, or lineage rather than a single family line.

title: Brand and product naming conventions - master names reference
description: Product names follow a small set of proven patterns: descriptive (General Motors), invented (Kodak — chosen because it meant nothing in any language), portmanteau blends, founder names (Ferrari, Toyota), and Latin or Greek roots (Sony from sonus, 'sound'; Volvo from volvo, 'I roll'). The pattern is picked for the market the product must survive in.

title: Place-naming conventions - master names reference
description: Settlers name new places the same few ways everywhere: after the homeland (New York, New Orleans), after a founder or patron (Washington, Johannesburg), after the landform (-ville 'town', -burg 'fort', -ford 'river crossing', -mouth), or by plain description (Oxford, 'ford for oxen'). Reading a place name is reading the priorities of the people who named it.

title: Naming taboos and honorifics - master names reference
description: Many cultures fence names with rules: imperial China forbade writing an emperor's given name (the naming taboo); Burmese names take honorifics U and Daw instead of Mr. and Mrs.; Malay names use bin/binti ('son/daughter of') rather than inherited surnames; Yoruba oriki praise names are earned, not given. The rulebook is part of the name.
